newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris reminds Kinshasa to protect foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Paris reminds Kinshasa to protect foreigners.

text.p: France on Wednesday reminded Laurent Kabila, self-proclaimed president of the new Democratic Republic of Congo, of his duty to protect foreign nationals after two Frenchmen were shot dead in Kinshasa on Tuesday.

"I solemnly remind the new authorities in Zaire that they are responsible to the international community for the safety of foreign residents, and as regards my particular concern, for the safety of French residents," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told Radio Monte Carlo.

But he and Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said they believed the shootings had been isolated incidents not meant as reprisals against France for its longtime friendship with the Mobutu Sese Seko, the toppled leader of former Zaire.
De Charette also urged Kabila, who changed his country's name after winning a civil war last week, to quickly hold democratic elections and take steps to assure aid to starving Hutu refugees.
Mobutu, a 66-year-old autocrat who had ruled since 1965, fled into exile after Kabila's rebel army swept across the vast central African country in just seven months.
The two Frenchmen were shot dead on Tuesday night by men in uniform as they were leaving a factory in Kinshasa's Limete district, according to a French diplomat.
The identity of the killers and the motive for the shootings were not immediately clear.
An undercurrent of anti-French feeling surfaced in Kinshasa in the final days of Mobutu's 32-year rule, residents say.
Rebel spokesmen had said before they took Kinshasa that hardline Mobutu loyalists might start killing foreigners to provoke intervention by their governments.
Toubon, in an interview on Europe 1 radio, noted that France was one of five Western nations with troops standing by in the nearby Republic of Congo.
But asked if French citizens should now leave the country, he said there was "no reason to panic".

Separately, de Charette said that "if Zaire -- excuse me, the Congo, wants to put this crisis behind it, it is time to organise a national unity government and ...a democratic process which alone can prepare it for the future".
He also said he was deeply troubled by Kabila's -- and the international community's -- apparent "indifference" to the fate of stranded ethnic Hutu refugees.
There have been reports of refugee massacres by Kabila's soldiers, and he has prevented international organisations from investigating the allegations.
As Kabila's forces conquered the country, France repeatedly urged international intervention to aid the refugees.
But a multinational force was never put in place despite approval by the United Nations after most of the refugees fled Zaire to return to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.
